source.title: Nexus scissor: enhance open-access language model safety by connection pruning
source.authors: Pei-Hua Mai; You-Jia Yang; Ran Yan; Yan Pang

record.tranche_reason: The study reports harmful-compliance rates under named harmful fine-tuning and decoding attacks, but does not present an explicit replication of the original studies' procedures.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports ASR for BDFinetune and GenExploit on the original models and after Nexus Scissor; those results are recorded below. The paper also evaluates AutoDAN and Template attacks, but does not characterize them as compliant-prefill or suffix attacks, so those results are not assigned to a claim version. GLUE utility results, clustering analyses, and the naive-unlearning comparison do not measure the listed claim versions. The paper does not report fine-tuning example counts or attack-training settings for BDFinetune.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper, but Table 2's 'Origin' column reports harmful-compliance ASR on four aligned open models. The attacks are BDFinetune (harmful-demonstration fine-tuning, citing Qi et al.) and GenExploit (decoding-parameter changes), on AdvBench with a Qi-style GPT-4o judge (score >2). These are the study's own results on V1 and V4. The method is a related attack, not a replication: example counts and fine-tuning settings are not stated, and no no-attack baseline is reported. The Nexus Scissor rows measure the authors' mitigation, not the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that Nexus Scissor (unlearning harmful knowledge-graph links) cuts average ASR by over 91% across four attacks with GLUE utility loss within 2%. It also gives at least 43% lower ASR and about 5% higher utility than naive unlearning (unLER). They do not draw conclusions about shallow alignment itself.
record.recipe_differences: The study's main method extracts harmful responses, builds and clusters knowledge triplets, then uses gradient ascent with a KL term to prune connections. Its BDFinetune attack is named as an attack method, but the paper does not state that it reproduces the original fine-tuning procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success differs across models and between Origin and Nexus Scissor checkpoints. The paper also reports that evaluation depends on the harmfulness scoring method in Table 4.
record.problems: The paper does not state BDFinetune attack data counts or fine-tuning settings, and it reports no uncertainty estimates for the ASRs. The measured ASR depends on a harmfulness-score threshold and the paper notes differences among judges.
record.rows_left_out: No results for V1 or V4 were left out. AutoDAN and Template attack results in Table 2 were omitted because the text does not identify them as harmful fine-tuning, decoding-parameter changes, compliant-start prefilling, or suffix attacks.

untested.parts: How few examples suffice (data count not reported); comparison with a no-attack baseline.
Compliant-start prefilling and adversarial suffixes. AutoDAN and template prompts are not prefill or suffix attacks as described.
Not tested; the paper only speculates about neuron localization as future work.
Not tested; Nexus Scissor is knowledge unlearning with no per-position analysis.

missing.what: Origin-model BDFinetune ASR under three other judges. LLaMA-2-7b: 87.50/94.81/92.88; LLaMA-2-13b: 50.96/54.03/49.23; LLaMA-3-8b: 44.42/59.62/47.88; Phi-3-14b: 87.69/95.77/92.88 (LLaMA Guard 2, LLaMA Guard 3, Beaver-Dam-7B). Shows judge dependence of the V1 numbers.
Per-category harmfulness scores (1–5) of origin models under BDFinetune on ForbidQ, 9 scenarios, 30 samples each; read from the figure only.

record.verdict_notes: The attack results are incidental baselines for a defense paper. No no-attack ASR is reported, BDFinetune data size and hyperparameters are not given, and there is no uncertainty. The reader's limits_scope labels based on post-defense rows were removed: a defense lowering ASR does not qualify V1 or V4. AutoDAN and Template results are reasonably excluded from V4.

versions.untested_parts: The number of harmful examples and fine-tuning settings are not stated; the results do not establish that a few to a few hundred examples remove refusal almost entirely.
The study tests GenExploit, described as changing decoding parameters. It does not test compliant-start prefilling or adversarial suffixes.
